items.title: Happy Beings, Suffering Beings, and Neither Is Ever Truly Safe

items.zh: 若諸有情，十資身具之所攝養，無所匱乏，身康無病，年未衰老，名為有樂有情世間。與此相違，當知有苦有情世間。世間眾生，少分有樂，多分有苦。
items.en: Those beings sustained by the ten requisites of life, lacking nothing, healthy and free of illness, not yet aged — these are called the happy beings of the world. The reverse of this should be known as the suffering beings of the world. Among the world's beings, only a small portion are happy; the great majority suffer.

items.zh: 諸有有樂有情世間，常懷恐怖。勿我財寶王所侵奪，廣說乃至勿由此緣遭諸苦難。勿或風熱於內發動，乃至或人或非人等侵損我耶。如是懼慮未來財寶變壞之苦及身壞苦，心常怖畏。
items.en: All the happy beings of the world constantly harbour fear: may my wealth not be seized by the state, and so on, down to — may I not, through such causes, encounter any misfortune. May the wind or heat within my body not become disturbed, nor may I be harmed by a human or non-human being. Thus, dreading the future suffering of wealth's ruin and the body's decline, the mind is constantly fearful.

items.zh: 諸有有苦有情世間，現為眾苦逼切身心，有苦、有憂、有愁、有箭、有諸擾惱，恒不安住。如是故言：常有怖世間，眾生恒所厭；於未生眾苦，或復已生中。由是因緣，彼天現見諸有有樂有情世間，樂非決定。請問如來，有決定樂無怖畏處。
items.en: All the suffering beings of the world are, at present, pressed in body and mind by manifold suffering — afflicted with pain, worry, grief, a lodged arrow, and every kind of disturbance, never settled or at rest. For this reason, the deity, seeing directly that even the world's happy beings have no decisive happiness, asked the Tathāgata: is there any place of decisive happiness, free of fear?

items.zh: 爾時世尊，即為彼天方便示現，惟聖教中有如是處，非諸外道。

items.title: Two Failed Paths: Ignorance of Desire's Faults, and Mistaking the Formless Peak for Freedom

items.zh: 謂如有一，住正法外所有沙門、或婆羅門，於現法中及當來世諸欲過患不如實知。由不知故，悕求未來諸欲差別；捨現法欲，求後法欲，精勤受學所有禁戒。雖復安住如是禁戒，然無智慧，不護根門，不守正念，無常委念，乃至廣說。
items.en: It refers to one — an ascetic or brahmin dwelling outside the true Dharma — who does not truly understand desire's faults, whether in this present life or lives to come. Because of this ignorance, they seek instead the varieties of future desire, abandoning present desire in hope of desire in a later existence, diligently undertaking whatever precepts they hold. Yet, abiding in such precepts, they lack wisdom, do not guard the sense-doors, do not maintain mindfulness, and never sustain it continuously and earnestly — and so on, as explained at length.

items.zh: 彼不調攝諸根門故，於他所惠少小利養及與恭敬尚生愛味，隨起戀著，何況廣大。如是精勤受禁戒者，遠離智慧、密護根門，於現法欲尚不能斷，況後法欲。
又即於彼，有一沙門、若婆羅門，於欲過患粗了知故，能越現法後法諸欲，而復欣求上離欲地。於非解脫起解脫想，斷棄諸欲便臻遠離。彼由精勤數多修習正思惟故，離欲欲界，乃至離欲無所有處。由此因緣，捨下自體，愛上自體。
items.en: And again, among them, there is an ascetic or brahmin who, having gained a coarse understanding of desire's faults, is able to transcend desire both present and future, and comes to long instead for the higher grounds free of desire. Mistaking what is not liberation for liberation, they cut off and abandon the desires, believing themselves thereby to reach true seclusion. Through diligent, sustained cultivation of this correct-seeming reflection, they become free of desire for the sense-desire realm, and on through freedom from desire even for the sphere of nothingness. By this cause, they abandon the lower states of being and come to cherish the higher ones instead.

items.title: Why Even the Highest Attainment Fails, and the Buddha's Precise Threefold Answer

items.zh: 由愛彼故，於當來世尚不解脫下地自體，何況上地。如是棄捨財寶自體迷失道者，雖復安住勇猛精勤，而不能得一向快樂無怖畏處。何以故？彼外道師尚於是處不見不識，況能為彼諸弟子等當廣開示。如是外道師及弟子所制論中，決定無有眾苦邊際。
items.en: Because of this very attachment, in future lives one is not even freed from the lower state of existence, let alone the higher. Thus, those who abandon wealth and self yet have lost the true path, however courageously and diligently they persevere, are unable to attain a state of decisive happiness free of fear. Why is this so? Because these teachers themselves neither see nor know that place — how much less could they fully disclose it to their disciples? In the treatises composed by such teachers and disciples alike, there is decidedly no reaching the very limit of suffering.

items.zh: 與此相違，善說正法毘柰耶中，當知具足一切義利，乃至定有眾苦邊際。依此密意，佛為彼天說如是言：天！我觀解脫，不離智精進，不離攝諸根，不離一切捨。
items.en: The reverse holds within the well-taught true Dharma and discipline: know that it is complete with every genuine benefit, and that the very limit of suffering is indeed found within it. Resting on this underlying intent, the Buddha spoke thus to the deity: Deity, as I observe it, liberation is never apart from wisdom and diligence, never apart from restraining the senses, and never apart from relinquishing everything entirely.

items.zh: 復次，今當略辨上所說義。謂為顯示惡說邪法毘柰耶中，師及弟子皆有衰損；善說
正法毘柰耶中，皆具吉祥，於一切苦能證邊際。當知是名此中略義。
items.en: [The commentarial gloss (披尋記) explains:] Rightly and diligently cultivating the practice of yoga through hearing, reflection, and meditation is called "wisdom and diligence" — this rules out the non-Buddhist path of taking up precepts alone, without wisdom. Closely guarding the sense-doors, cultivating restraint of the faculties, is called "restraining the senses" — this rules out the non-Buddhist failure to guard the senses at all. Being free of craving for all three realms, taking no further rebirth, is called "relinquishing everything entirely" — this rules out the non-Buddhist error of abandoning the lower state of being only to cherish the higher one instead.

items.title: The Deity's Praise: Four Extraordinary Qualities, and Fascicle 17 Concludes

items.zh: 爾時彼天聞佛世尊答所請問，歡喜踊躍，即以四種無上功德讚歎如來。謂佛世尊難出現故，出已能成利他行故，亦能建立自利德故，於自他利離染心故。
items.en: At that time, the deity, having heard the Blessed One answer the question asked, was filled with joy, and praised the Tathāgata with four unsurpassed qualities: that the Blessed Buddha is difficult to encounter in the world; that, having appeared, he is able to accomplish the benefit of others; that he is also able to establish the virtue of his own benefit; and that, in benefiting both self and other, his mind remains entirely free of defilement.

items.zh: 我觀極久遠梵，志般涅槃者，此讚世尊難出現德。已過諸怨者，此讚世尊利他行德。已過諸怖者，此讚世尊建自利德。超世間貪欲者，此讚世尊於自他利離染心德。
items.en: "As I have observed across a very long time, one who has left desire behind has attained final nirvāṇa" praises the Blessed One's quality of being difficult to encounter. "Already passed beyond every enmity" praises his quality of benefiting others. "Already passed beyond every fear" praises his quality of establishing his own benefit. "Transcending the world's own craving" praises his quality of remaining free of defilement in benefiting both self and other.

items.zh: 當知復有三種差別。謂難出現故，難可見故，建立自利利他行故。見者則能成就大義。成大義者，離染心故，遍一切生亦無眾罪。如是眾德，諸佛世尊最為殊勝，故以此相讚歎如來。
items.en: Know that there is, further, a threefold distinction: being difficult to encounter, being difficult to see, and establishing the practice of benefiting both self and other. One who sees him thereby accomplishes great benefit. This great benefit accomplished means: because the mind is free of defilement, one incurs no fault whatsoever throughout every future rebirth. Virtues such as these make the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, supreme above all — and it is with marks such as these that the Tathāgata is praised.

blocks.text: The last day of fascicle 17. The Buddha explains why fear pervades the world, why other paths fail to end it, and the deva praises him. A few short passages are untranslated.

"Those sustained by the ten requisites of life, lacking nothing, healthy, not yet aged: these are the happy beings of the world." Only a few are happy; the great majority suffer. Master Cháng Bǎi: everyone feels they suffer most. Suffering is like an arrow: Venerable Miào Jìng: "when affliction comes, it keeps chasing one without release." And even the happy have no **decisive happiness**: happiness that cannot be destroyed, with which the mind would be without fear.

Some give up present pleasure in hope of pleasure in a later existence, and keep strict precepts; but they lack wisdom, do not guard the senses, and do not keep mindfulness. Others reach the peak of existence in meditation and mistake it for liberation. Master Cháng Bǎi: such meditation only subdues the active afflictions, "like a stone pressing on grass: the roots are not cut, and when the spring wind blows it grows again."

Their teachers "neither see nor know that place; how much less could they disclose it to their disciples?" In their treatises "there is decidedly no reaching the very limit of suffering." Venerable Miào Jìng: the stronger such concentration, the stronger the sense of self.

Hence the threefold answer of Day 143: wisdom with diligence, restraint of the senses, relinquishing everything. Together they are the three trainings again: precepts in restraint, concentration in diligence, wisdom in seeing.

The deity praises the Buddha with four qualities: rarity; benefiting others; perfect self-benefit; freedom from defilement in benefiting both. Master Cháng Bǎi on "beyond every enmity": the Buddha practises great compassion; "the benevolent have no enemies." Venerable Miào Jìng on "seeing" the Buddha: it means realisation, not merely meeting him.
This fascicle has been practical throughout: how a renunciant lives, how desire grows and is stilled, how the floods are crossed. The essential-body verses continue in fascicle 18.

quiz.q: How does the treatise define the happy beings of the world, and what is the proportion of happy to suffering beings?
options: sustained by the ten requisites, lacking nothing, healthy, not yet aged; only a small portion are happy, the great majority suffer
beings in heaven; most are happy
quiz.why: "Those beings sustained by the ten requisites of life, lacking nothing, healthy and free of illness, not yet aged — these are called the happy beings of the world... Among the world's beings, only a small portion are happy; the great majority suffer." Master Cháng Bǎi: everyone feels they suffer most, though their sufferings differ.

quiz.q: Suffering beings are afflicted with "pain, worry, grief, a lodged arrow." How does Venerable Miào Jìng explain "arrow"?
options: suffering that follows and never lets go — once it comes it keeps pursuing, with no escape
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: the arrow means suffering that follows one and never lets go — when affliction comes, it keeps chasing one without release; that is called the arrow.

quiz.q: The deity asks for "a place of decisive happiness, free of fear." What is decisive happiness, per Venerable Miào Jìng?
options: happiness that cannot be destroyed — with it, the mind has no fear
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: it is happiness that cannot be destroyed; with such happiness, the mind is without fear. Seeing that even the happy beings' happiness is not decisive, the deity asked the Buddha.

quiz.q: What does the treatise say is wrong with the first kind of non-Buddhist ascetic or brahmin?
options: not truly knowing desire's faults, abandoning present desire to seek future desire through precepts; though keeping them, lacking wisdom, unguarded senses, no mindfulness
quiz.why: "Abandoning present desire in hope of desire in a later existence, diligently undertaking whatever precepts they hold. Yet, abiding in such precepts, they lack wisdom, do not guard the sense-doors, do not maintain mindfulness." Venerable Miào Jìng: continuous mindfulness is guarding it without interruption; earnest mindfulness is guarding the mind with deep care.

quiz.q: The second kind climbs to the sphere of nothingness yet mistakes it for liberation. What simile does Master Cháng Bǎi use, and how does it differ from the note's?
options: a flower in a mirror; the same
the moon in water; the same
clouds in the sky; the note omits it
a stone pressing on grass — the roots are not cut, and it grows back in spring; the note writes grass cut but not uprooted
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: their meditation can only subdue the lower grounds' active afflictions, not sever the seeds — like a stone pressing on grass: the roots are not cut, and when the spring wind blows it grows again. The note's "grass cut but never pulled up" is a different image.

quiz.q: Why does the treatise say these non-Buddhists cannot attain a state of decisive happiness free of fear?
options: their teachers neither see nor know that place, let alone disclose it to disciples; their treatises decidedly contain no limit of suffering
quiz.why: "These teachers themselves neither see nor know that place — how much less could they fully disclose it to their disciples? In the treatises composed by such teachers and disciples alike, there is decidedly no reaching the very limit of suffering." Venerable Miào Jìng: the stronger the concentration, the greater the self-clinging.

quiz.q: The deity praises the Tathāgata with four unsurpassed qualities. How does the treatise match the verse's phrases to them?
options: beyond enmity is self-benefit, beyond fear is benefit of others
the opening praises rarity; "beyond every enmity," benefiting others; "beyond every fear," establishing self-benefit; "transcending the world's craving," freedom from defilement in both
quiz.why: The treatise matches the phrases in turn to rarity, benefiting others, establishing self-benefit, and freedom from defilement in benefiting both. Master Cháng Bǎi: "beyond every enmity" means the Buddha practices great compassion — the benevolent have no enemies, so surely no one resents him.
